passage:
"Team, I have an idea," Ojas said. "What if we sent clients a short monthly video instead of a long report?"
"It won't work," said Anirban, not looking up from his screen. "I'm just being realistic."
"Why not?"
"People don't watch videos."
"Have you tried it?"
"No. But I know how these things go."
Ojas kept his voice light. "Last month you said the same about the new template. We tried it and clients liked it."
Anirban shrugged. "Lucky."
"Could we try one video and see? If it flops, we've lost an afternoon."
"I'm being realistic, Ojas. Somebody has to be."
The room went quiet. Ojas noticed that Anirban's notebook page was blank.

qa.q: What idea did Ojas propose?
qa.a: Ojas proposed sending clients a short monthly video instead of a long report.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling as Anirban kept dismissing ideas?
qa.a: Ojas was patient but frustrated, keeping a light voice and pointing out the earlier template success.

qa.q: What small step could Ojas suggest to test the idea without a big risk?
qa.a: Ojas could ask the team to try one video and see, since the cost if it flops is only an afternoon.

qa.q: Why might Anirban keep saying he is being realistic?
qa.a: Anirban may fear being wrong or blamed, so it feels safer not to try. Saying realistic makes not trying sound wise.

grounding: A colleague says he is just being realistic to every idea and never tries; cynicism can pass for wisdom, but real realism still risks something.

passage:
I've worked next to Shreya for two years. Whenever someone proposes something new she says, "I'm just being realistic," and lists three reasons it will fail. The reasons are usually sensible. But I've noticed she never proposes anything herself, and never tries the small version. When I asked her about it once, she said, "If I don't try, I can't be wrong."
That stayed with me. Real realism, I think, would say, "The odds are poor, so here's a small test." Shreya's version ends in a shrug. I don't know what happened to make her so careful. Maybe something burned her once. I'm Sachin, and lately I bring her small, low-risk questions and see if she'll play.

qa.q: How long has Sachin worked next to Shreya?
qa.a: Sachin has worked next to Shreya for two years.

qa.q: What is Sachin feeling about Shreya's habit?
qa.a: Sachin feels puzzled and a little sympathetic, wondering what made Shreya so careful, while noticing the pattern.

qa.q: What is Sachin doing to invite Shreya to take small risks?
qa.a: Sachin brings Shreya small, low-risk questions and sees if she will play, instead of arguing about her reasons.

qa.q: What might Shreya be protecting herself from when she says that if she doesn't try she can't be wrong?
qa.a: Shreya may be protecting herself from failing or looking foolish. Sachin guesses she may have been burned once.

grounding: A colleague says she is just being realistic whenever an idea appears and never tries; cynicism can pass for wisdom.

passage:
Team lead's note, marketing, Thursday.
In this morning's meeting Kalyani proposed a small trial: a weekend stall at the college fest to reach students. Before she'd finished, Sonali said, "I'm just being realistic, nobody visits stalls anymore." It's the fourth idea this month she's met the same way. Last week it was the podcast; before that, the new newsletter.
Sonali is sharp and experienced, and some of her concerns are fair. But I've noticed she never suggests an alternative or offers to try a small version. Kalyani went quiet and closed her notebook.
After the meeting I asked Sonali: "If you were running the stall, what would make it worth trying?" She hesitated, then gave two good suggestions. I've asked her and Kalyani to plan a one-day trial together. I'll check in on both on Monday.

qa.q: What did Kalyani propose in the morning meeting?
qa.a: A small trial: a weekend stall at the college fest to reach students.

qa.q: How did Kalyani seem to feel after Sonali's comment?
qa.a: Kalyani seemed deflated and discouraged, going quiet and closing her notebook.

qa.q: What did the team lead do next that might help?
qa.a: They asked Sonali what would make the stall worth trying and paired her with Kalyani on a one-day trial, turning criticism into shared risk.

qa.q: How might Sonali see her own 'realism'?
qa.a: She probably thinks she's protecting the team from wasted effort, without noticing she never risks anything herself.

grounding: Shows a team lead noticing a colleague who calls herself realistic about every idea but never tries, and inviting her to take a small risk.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Minakshi did it again today. Rohan pitched the idea of a lunch-and-learn for the new joiners, and Minakshi said, "I'm just being realistic, people won't come." She said the same about the mentoring scheme in June and the suggestion box in August.
Everyone nods when she says it. She sounds wise. For a long time I thought she was.
But today I added it up. In two years I've never seen her try a single thing, even a small one. Real realism would be, "People might not come, so let's try one session and see." That still risks something.
I think her "realistic" is really a way of never being wrong.
I'm not going to argue with her in meetings. But tomorrow I'll tell Rohan I'll help him run the first session anyway.
Kamal

qa.q: What did Rohan pitch today?
qa.a: A lunch-and-learn for the new joiners.

qa.q: What did Kamal realise about Minakshi's comments?
qa.a: Kamal felt disappointed and a little uneasy, realising that the 'realism' was really a way of never being wrong and never trying.

qa.q: What small step does Kamal plan, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Kamal plans to help Rohan run the first session, which tests the idea in a small way instead of arguing in meetings.

qa.q: How might Rohan feel when Kamal offers to help?
qa.a: Rohan would probably feel encouraged and relieved after having his idea dismissed.

grounding: Shows a person noticing a colleague's constant 'I'm just being realistic' is cynicism that never risks anything.

passage:
Jaya: idea. what if we run a weekend pottery stall at the flea market? just once
Ira: realistically? nobody buys pottery
Jaya: some people do. the tea mugs sold out at Diwali
Ira: that was a fluke. I'm just being realistic
Jaya: you said that about the workshop too. and the online shop
Ira: and I was right, we never did them
Jaya: we never did them because you said they wouldn't work 😅
Ira: …
Jaya: ok real question. what WOULD make a stall worth it?
Ira: maybe if we only took mugs and small bowls. and shared the table cost with someone
Jaya: see, that's realistic AND it risks something
Ira: fine. one Sunday. but I'm not smiling at customers
Jaya: deal 🙂

qa.q: What sold out at Diwali?
qa.a: The tea mugs.

qa.q: What was Jaya thinking in the message 'we never did them because you said they wouldn't work'?
qa.a: Jaya seemed amused but also frustrated, noticing that Ira's realism was stopping them from ever trying.

qa.q: How did Jaya's question help Ira move?
qa.a: Asking what would make the stall worth it turned Ira's doubts into practical conditions, so Ira agreed to one Sunday.

qa.q: How might Ira see this 'realism'?
qa.a: Ira probably thinks it is sensible and protective, not noticing it has kept them from trying anything.

grounding: Shows a person noticing that a friend's constant 'I'm just being realistic' is closer to cynicism, and inviting a small risk.

passage: In the staff room of the government school at Rampura, Ishita suggested turning the empty storeroom into a reading corner. Sarita, who had taught there eleven years, didn't look up from her register. "Be realistic. The children won't come, the books will get stolen, and the headmaster won't sanction anything." Ishita had heard the same line about the kitchen garden in July and the morning radio quiz in August. Each time Sarita sounded wise. Each time nothing was tried. Ishita watched her thumb the edge of the register and remembered hearing that Sarita's own library plan had been scrapped years ago. That evening Ishita cleared one shelf herself and brought six books from home. By Friday, four children were reading there at lunch. Sarita paused in the doorway, then walked on without a word.

qa.q: How long had Sarita taught at the school?
qa.a: She had taught there eleven years.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as Sarita called the idea unrealistic again?
qa.a: Ishita felt frustrated but also curious, noticing that Sarita's "realism" always ended with nothing being tried.

qa.q: What did Ishita's small test show?
qa.a: Clearing one shelf with six books risked very little, and four children reading by Friday gave real evidence instead of predictions.

qa.q: What might Sarita have felt pausing in the doorway?
qa.a: She may have felt surprise mixed with an old sting, perhaps remembering her own library plan that was scrapped.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing that a colleague's constant "realism" is really cynicism that never tries anything.
